sections.title: Front matter

summary.text: Front matter, table of contents, acronyms, glossary, executive summary, audience-specific reading paths matrix, and Section 1.1 opening for the WHO–ITU Draft v1.0 Reference Architecture and Guidance for Digital Public Infrastructure for the Health Sector (DPI-H). Introduces DPI-H as shared, standards-based digital resources serving multiple health agency functions; defines Resilient Essential Data and Digital Health Infrastructure (REDDHI); outlines the TOGAF and ArchiMate enterprise-architecture approach anchored on seven priority health goals; explains how the guidance extends the WHO–ITU Digital Health Platform Handbook, OpenHIE Architecture, and WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide (DIIG); and provides a section-by-section relevance matrix for policy makers, DPI authorities, enterprise architects, development partners, and procurement teams.

sections.title: Why health needs more than foundational DPI

summary.text: Section 1.2 explains why the health sector requires capabilities beyond general-purpose foundational DPIs (identity, payments, and data exchange): foundational DPIs intentionally leave sector-specific logic to consuming sectors, and in many low- and middle-income countries foundational DPIs remain nascent or absent while care delivery, disease surveillance, health financing, and supply chain management must operate immediately without creating permanent parallel silos.

sections.title: Identity DPI and Identification in Healthcare

summary.text: Section 1.2.1 and Box 1.2 examine why foundational identity DPI is necessary but insufficient on its own for healthcare, identifying six health-specific requirements: (1) universal coverage across newborns prior to civil registration, refugees, undocumented migrants, and marginalised groups to preserve care continuity and surveillance denominators; (2) purpose context such as scheme enrolment and service entitlements; (3) granular health privacy and consent management; (4) probabilistic clinical matching, duplicate detection, and family linkage for undocumented patients; (5) coexistence of multiple context-specific health identifiers; and (6) cross-border recognition. Positions the Client Registry as the health sector's identity DPI bridging foundational identity with health-specific needs.

summary.text: Section 1.3.1 analyses the technical, economic, and political-economy costs of vertical, programme-driven digital health fragmentation across HIV, immunisation, maternal health, TB, and malaria silos. sections.title: Value Across Stakeholders

summary.text: Section 1.3.3 summarises how shared DPI-H distributes value across ten stakeholder groups: patients (continuity of clinical history, identity, and entitlements), health workers (reduced duplicate data entry and richer point-of-care context), health programme managers (cross-programme analytics and planning), Ministries of Health (ecosystem visibility and governance), Ministries of Finance (expenditure transparency, fraud detection, and timely provider payment evidence), development partners and donors (investments outlasting single funding cycles), researchers (consistent consented datasets), the commercial sector (value-added innovation on shared foundations), DPI Authorities (extended utility of foundational DPI), and the health system overall, while enabling rather than replacing point-of-service applications.

sections.title: DPI-H Principles

summary.text: Section 1.4 defines six core principles governing how DPI-H is conceived, built, governed, and sustained: Interoperability (data and system exchange extensible without disruption), Reusability (shared functionality and data across programmes), Open Standards and Specifications (SDO-governed open APIs and standards avoiding proprietary lock-in), Public Governance (accountable public-interest stewardship and oversight regardless of whether components are operated by public, private, or NGO actors), Security and Privacy (zero-trust security, privacy as a right, and service resilience by design), and Autonomy and Sovereignty (national ownership and control free from external jurisdictional dependency).

sections.title: Trustworthy AI in a health setting

summary.text: Section 5.4.2 explains that trustworthy AI in healthcare must be earned through evidence of effectiveness, safety, transparency about limitations, human accountability, fairness, and meaningful human oversight. Advises decision-makers to interrogate vendor claims (task specificity, data dependencies, evaluation evidence, error accountability, and governance) and conduct recurring evaluations ('evals') against representative cases and explicit criteria before and during deployment, referencing the Council of Europe AI Framework Convention (CETS No. 225), national AI statutes in the Republic of Korea (Act No. 20676) and Peru (Ley N.º 31814), and WHO AI resources.

sections.extract: 154 Closely related to readiness is the question of what makes AI trustworthy in a health setting. 155 Trustworthy AI is not a quality a product can assert for itself; it is earned through evidence that a 156 system is effective for its stated purpose, safe, transparent about its limitations, accountable to 157 identifiable people, fair across the populations it serves, and subject to meaningful human 158 oversight.

sections.title: Appendix E: Health Goals to DPI Mapping

summary.text: Appendix E ('Health Goals to DPI Mapping') explains how the seven priority health goals map through stakeholder value, business capabilities, and application services to shared DPI-H and foundational-DPI components: Goal 1 (Build Trusted Data Foundations) serves as the shared REDDHI foundation reused by all other goals; Goal 2 (Health Workforce) centres on the Health Workforce, Facility, and Terminology Services; Goal 3 (Quality and Continuity of Care) reuses core registries and the LHR while introducing the CDSE; Goal 4 (Trusted Personal Health Records) realises person-controlled access over the LHR, registries, and foundational trust/consent services; Goal 5 (Supply Chain Management) adds the Product and Supplier Registries; Goal 6 (Health Financing) references Section 2.4.2 and the full financing mapping spreadsheet; and Goal 7 (Climate and Epidemic Resilience) combines the PHSP and shared health registries with cross-sectoral weather, climate, and environmental data infrastructure.

sections.title: Appendix F: Semantic Governance Infrastructure: capability details

summary.text: Appendix F ('Semantic Governance Infrastructure: capability details'), Table F ('SGI Capability Details'), and Figure A.1 break down the five semantic governance capability categories introduced in Section 3.4.5—Intake (change requests, upstream release ingestion, deprecation handling, triage, queue management), Authoring and publication (content authoring, review workflow, approval, versioning, release packaging, business rule enforcement, audit trail), Monitoring (governance compliance, content quality, currency/staleness, uptake telemetry, reporting/alerting), Distribution (multi-modal delivery, access control, reliability, versioned canonical URLs, endpoint discovery), and Consumption (discovery, retrieval, integration tooling, change subscription, maintainer feedback)—across the roles (stakeholders, authors, owners), rules, and policies that govern them.
